After high school, I attended a local community college on a part‑time basis while raising my own family. I earned a handful of college credits—mostly in history and English—but never finished a degree. Education was always a passion, even if it never led to a diploma on my transcript.

I never held a job outside the home. My husband worked as a machinist at the nearby factory, and I took care of our house, our three children, and later, our grandchildren. Even after retirement, I stayed at home, managing the household and keeping the family’s traditions alive. I never had a driver’s license, and I have always relied on public transit or family members for transportation. My home, which I bought with a mortgage in 1965, has been my sanctuary for 58 years; the walls have seen my children grow up, the house has survived a few harsh winters, and the garden in the back has been a place of quiet reflection.

Living with a hearing impairment and a mental and emotional disability has shaped much of my daily routine. I use a cane or walker for short distances, and I have a transferable wheelchair for longer trips. My disability limits my daily travel—most of my outings are short, close to home, and often accompanied by my daughter or a friend. My days are filled with the quiet sounds of my garden, the occasional call from my grandchildren, and the soft music that I used to listen to on the radio. I’m 21, a white male who’s been living in the same house for the past 18 years. The house is a two‑story, single‑family home that I own with a mortgage—my parents bought it when I was a child, and I’ve grown up in the same rooms and kitchen as they did. I’m the eldest son in our household, and we’re all still living under the same roof, even though I’ve started carving out my own life.

I’m currently a full‑time college student at a four‑year university, majoring in business administration. I’ve taken some college credits before but never finished a degree, so I’m back on the path to a bachelor’s now. My schedule is tight: I attend classes Monday through Friday, but I also work part‑time to help pay for tuition and living expenses.

I work in retail trade, specifically in a warehouse where I help move and load inventory. The job’s classified under transportation and material moving occupations, so I spend a lot of time in a truck or van as a passenger, getting to the warehouse and back. I work 12 hours a week, split over two days—Tuesday and Thursday—so I can keep my evenings free for study and rest. I drive to the job, but I also use public transit three to four times a week when I need to get around the city or to visit family. I have a driver’s license and a vehicle that’s always available for me when I use public transit, which helps a lot because my disability—autism spectrum disorder and ADHD—sometimes makes navigating unfamiliar routes or waiting for rides stressful. The vehicle and the public transit system together help me get where I need to go without too much friction.

Because of my autism and ADHD, daily travel can be limiting. I find that I need a predictable routine and familiar routes, so I stick to the same travel plans whenever possible. I’ve learned to plan my trips in advance, use the same bus lines, and keep my phone handy for navigation. My disability also means I often rely on a combination of public transit and my car to get to work and to my classes. Even though I have a vehicle, I still use public transit regularly because it’s more efficient for certain trips and because it gives me a break from driving.

Outside of school and work, I don’t volunteer regularly, but I do spend time with my family and friends, and I’ve been learning to manage my time better. I’m still figuring out the best ways to balance my responsibilities, but I’m proud of the progress I’ve made so far.

I’m Jose Ramirez, 25, and I grew up in a small, tight‑knit community in southern Texas. I’m proud to say I’m both Hispanic/Latino and identify as White—my parents are Mexican immigrants, and we’ve always celebrated our cultural heritage while living in this predominantly white town. I finished high school with a GED, but I’ve always struggled with a learning disability that makes reading and organization a daily challenge. The good news is that I’ve learned strategies to manage it, and I’m now a part‑time student at a local community college, taking courses in business and culinary arts.

I work in the food preparation and serving sector at a nearby grocery store, which falls under the retail trade industry. I clock in about 21 hours each week, three days a week, and I always arrive by walking. I don’t own a car and don’t have a driver’s license, so I rely on my good legs and a sturdy pair of sneakers to get to work. Walking also gives me a chance to clear my head before the rush starts. I’m the older brother in my household, and we’ve lived in the house I own with a mortgage for the past year. I’m the one who keeps the lights on and the fridge stocked, and I’m always ready to help my sister or cousin with homework or household chores.

Because my disability doesn’t limit my daily travel, I can move around the neighborhood without a cane or walker. I never use public transit to get to work, and I don’t have a toll payment method—my life is pretty simple. I love the rhythm of my routine: a quick walk to the store, a few hours of cooking and serving, and then back home to study, practice my Spanish, and plan for the next week. My life is a mix of hard work, learning, and family, and I wouldn’t trade it for anything.

Education has always been important to me. I earned some college credits in business administration but never completed a degree. My name is Thomas, but most people call me Tom. I’m 50 years old and was born and raised on the Navajo reservation in Arizona. I work 50 hours a week, five days a week, and I don’t have a fixed workplace. I travel to different schools, community centers, and training facilities each day, using the train five or more times a week to get to my various assignments. I own the house where I have lived for the past 11 years, and I have a driver’s license, but I don’t own a vehicle. I rely on public transit and occasional ride‑shares to get around. I was born in 1924 in a small town in Alabama and grew up in a close‑knit African‑American community. After high school, I earned a scholarship to Howard University, where I completed a bachelor’s degree in Sociology in 1946 and went on to earn a Ph.D. in Social Work in 1952. I spent the next three decades as a professor of social work at a community college in Washington, D.C., mentoring countless students and conducting research on urban poverty and family dynamics. I retired in 2000, after 30 years of teaching and community service.

In 2008, I moved to my current home in a quiet suburban neighborhood in Maryland. I’ve lived there for the past 15 years, and it’s the place where my family and I have celebrated birthdays, holidays, and the milestones of my grandchildren. I own the house outright and have taken pride in keeping it well maintained, despite the challenges I face.

I’m 99 years old now, a proud African‑American male who has seen so many changes in the world. I am the father of my daughter, who is now a high‑school senior, and the grandfather of a 13‑year‑old son who is preparing for his freshman year. I still keep in touch with my daughter’s friends and my grandson’s teachers, often through phone calls or video chats, even though I’m both visually and hearing impaired. I use a cane for mobility and a walker for longer distances. Because of my disabilities, I’m unable to drive and I don’t have a driver’s license. I also don’t own a vehicle, so I rely on public transit for any trips that I must make, although my travel is limited to essential errands and visits to my doctor’s office.

I am no longer employed; I’m retired and spend most of my days reading, listening to music on a screen‑reader, and keeping up with my family’s lives. I don’t volunteer regularly, and I don’t have any formal education enrollment at the moment. I don’t travel to work—my work was in the past—and I don’t have any current employer. I also don’t use toll payment methods or have any other transportation arrangements beyond the public transit system.

Despite the challenges that my visual and hearing impairments present, I find joy in the simple moments: watching the sunrise from my porch, hearing my grandson’s laughter as he plays video games, and feeling the rhythm of my cane as I walk to the mailbox. My life has been shaped by perseverance, faith, and the love of my family.

I don’t have any visual or hearing impairments, and I don’t use a cane, walker, or wheelchair. I have a driver’s license, but I rely almost exclusively on public transit to get to work. My commute is a steady rhythm that keeps me connected to my students and my community.

I’m not Hispanic or Latino, and I don’t volunteer regularly, but I find fulfillment in teaching and in the sense of purpose it brings. The combination of my education, my role in technology, and my ability to navigate the public transit system lets me maintain a stable life while managing my mental and emotional health.
